Chapter 01

The whole system, before the mathematics

The voice is evidence about a claimed student account. The system compares the sound of a natural whole-ID utterance with enrolled recordings. It requests a whole-name utterance only if the ID does not verify.

The operator first enters the seven-digit account independently. One ID attempt can verify it immediately. Otherwise, one name attempt receives the same kind of independent claim, distance and separation checks. If neither succeeds, the screen shows FAILED. A successful voice check then reaches payment and meal rules; it is not itself a meal-log entry.

Keep three questions separate throughout this manual: Is this a usable speech signal? Does it verify the entered identity? May that verified account receive this meal now? An energy detector answers only the first question. A low DTW distance is only part of the second. Payment and duplicate prevention answer the third.

Each chapter explains the concept, the actual implementation, and its limits. The figures and tables use saved MATLAB measurements. Code links refer to the source beside this HTML; the page itself remains readable with no server, internet connection, or external library.

Source: run_meal_system.m · verify_meal_workflow.m · preprocess_audio.m · speaker_verification_decision.m

Chapter 02

Samples, amplitude, time and frequency

A microphone converts changing air pressure to an electrical signal; the recorder stores a sequence of amplitude samples. Sample index n is not a time in seconds until a sampling rate is known. At 44,100 samples per second, sample 44,100 is approximately one second after sample zero. The amplitude values in the DSP code are floating-point, normalized PCM quantities.

x[n] = x_continuous(n / Fs)
t[n] = n / Fs
Duration ≈ number of samples / Fs

Frequency describes cycles per second. A sinusoid is a useful test signal, but speech is a changing mixture: periodic voiced excitation, vocal-tract resonances, consonant noise, and the room and microphone response. One frequency or one pitch estimate cannot identify a student reliably.

Nyquist is a bandwidth condition

A sampled signal can represent frequencies below half its sample rate without aliasing only if the input is suitably band-limited. The 8 kHz processing rate has a 4 kHz Nyquist boundary. It deliberately discards higher-frequency content; it does not preserve every possible speaker cue. The rate choice must therefore be checked by verification measurements.

For example, a 6 kHz sinusoid sampled directly at 8 kHz appears as a 2 kHz component. Filtering before downsampling prevents such out-of-band energy from folding into the retained band. A digital low-pass has a transition region, so “4 kHz boundary” does not mean an ideal brick-wall filter.

Three coordinate systems appear in the project

The recorder uses native-rate samples; preprocessing produces 8 kHz samples; MFCC produces feature frames every 10 ms. DTW aligns these feature frames. A reduction in waveform sample count does not automatically reduce the number of 10 ms feature frames or the DTW grid size.

Source: rational_resample_audio.m · extract_mfcc_dsp.m · dtw_distance_dsp.m

Chapter 03

Adaptive recording: detect speech, then its ending

Press Record and Verify, remain quiet during the initial ambient profile, and wait for SPEAK NOW. Say the complete ID naturally. The recorder watches short-time amplitude while recording. Once sustained speech has begun, a sustained low-energy pause can end recording before the eight-second limit.

The streaming detector uses non-overlapping 20 ms RMS frames at the actual recording rate. The noise floor is the RMS of all samples in the initial 0.5 s, not a median of short frames. The onset threshold is max(10⁻⁵, 3 × noise RMS); the continuation/end threshold is max(5 × 10⁻⁶, 1.8 × noise RMS). This two-threshold design is hysteresis. The optional streaming zero-crossing gate is off in the selected capture settings; the later DSP endpoint stage uses STE and ZCR.

Frame RMS = sqrt(mean(frame²))
Start: RMS exceeds the higher threshold for 0.12 s
Continue: RMS exceeds the lower threshold
Finish: enough speech has accumulated (0.25 s), then 0.8 s below the end threshold
Hard limit: stop at 8 s even if onset or ending is not detected

Requiring an onset to persist rejects a brief spike as a recording-start cue. The lower continuation threshold helps preserve softer syllables after a strong onset. The silence hangover tolerates a short internal pause. A long pause inside a slowly spoken ID can still end recording early; the timing is a practical operating choice, not a linguistic understanding of sentence completion.

The detector's 0.25 s accumulated-speech condition permits an early stop decision; it is different from the stricter live speech-duration quality check. No speech waits for the hard cap rather than declaring a successful recording. If polling observes a prefix after the end condition already occurred, the detector reports the earliest stopping sample so later sound does not extend the intended capture.

Instant Stop is separate from automatic speech end. It cancels the transaction. Cancellation flags remain visible while the active callback unwinds, and Record stays disabled until cleanup. An active-transaction guard prevents a second callback from starting a nested transaction.

The saved 31-student accuracy experiment uses archived recordings. It does not measure microphone timing, the frequency of early cutoffs, or field accuracy of automatic stopping. Deterministic waveform tests check the detector’s state transitions and sample timing.

Source: capture_voice_features.m · speech_capture_state.m · test_speech_capture_state.m · meal_verification_gui.m · test_gui_stop_controls.m

Chapter 04

Rational resampling and the polyphase filter

Live capture is configured for 44.1 kHz. The supplied recordings were principally 48 kHz stereo. Their copies are reduced to mono for the corpus and retain their original sample rate until preprocessing. The resampler calculates the ratio from the actual input rate; it never assumes every WAV is 44.1 kHz.

Fs_out / Fs_in = L / M, reduced to lowest integers
8,000 / 44,100 = 80 / 441
8,000 / 48,000 = 1 / 6

The conceptual sequence is interpolation by L, low-pass filtering, then decimation by M. Inserting zeros produces spectral images; decimation can alias frequencies. The low-pass deals with both. A polyphase implementation reorganizes the FIR calculations so it computes the needed output samples without naively constructing and filtering every zero-inserted sample.

rational_resample_audio uses MATLAB resample with a Kaiser-windowed FIR, filter-order parameter 20 and Kaiser beta 5. The reported prototype length is 2 × 20 × max(L,M) + 1: 17,641 taps for 80/441 and 241 for 1/6. These are prototype lengths, not an assertion that every output sample requires that many independent multiplications. The library compensates filter delay to keep the result aligned.

At 8 kHz, the same duration contains 81.86% fewer samples than at 44.1 kHz and 83.33% fewer than at 48 kHz. This reduces waveform-domain work and per-frame FFT size. The downstream frame hop remains 10 ms, so DTW still aligns approximately the same number of frames.

The observed rate comparison belongs to this corpus and its calibrated gates. It does not prove that 8 kHz is universally optimal or that all speaker information lies below 4 kHz.

Source: rational_resample_audio.m · experiment_variants.m

Source: sampling_rate_results.csv

Chapter 05

DC removal, RMS normalization and headroom

A constant DC offset increases measured energy without describing speech. The gain-control function subtracts the mean before measuring RMS. RMS summarizes average squared amplitude; peak normalization uses the single largest sample. RMS usually provides a more stable level reference, but squared samples still give large outliers substantial influence.

x₀[n] = x[n] − mean(x)
r = sqrt(mean(x₀[n]²))
g = min(0.05 / r, 40)
y[n] = g x₀[n]
If max(|y|) > 0.99: rescale the entire output by 0.99 / max(|y|)

If the input RMS is below 10⁻⁵, the function returns the DC-corrected signal without boosting it. Otherwise, an RMS of 0.01 gives gain 5 and an intended output RMS of 0.05. An RMS of 0.001 would need gain 50, but the cap limits it to 40, so the output RMS is at most 0.04 before headroom scaling. The cap and headroom mean the target is not guaranteed on every recording.

The headroom step is global rescaling, not a nonlinear sample-by-sample clipper. It prevents new clipping in that stage but cannot reconstruct a waveform already clipped by the microphone. The code applies AGC to the full capture before noise processing and again to the extracted speech region, whose RMS may differ after trimming silence.

Multiplying speech and noise by the same constant leaves their ratio unchanged. AGC is level control, not noise cancellation. Likewise, multiplying an archived waveform by a synthetic gain does not simulate the changes in room response and noise mix caused by moving a microphone.

Source: agc_normalize.m · preprocess_audio.m

Source: synthetic_agc_results.csv

Chapter 06

Short-time Fourier analysis and windows

The DFT represents a finite frame as a weighted sum of complex sinusoids. Its magnitude describes how strongly each frequency bin contributes, and its angle describes phase. Speech changes over time, so one transform of a whole sentence would average together different sounds. Short-time analysis moves a window over the waveform and transforms each frame separately.

X[k] = Σ x[n] w[n] exp(−j 2πkn / NFFT)
Bin frequency f[k] = k Fs / NFFT
Power-like quantity P[k] = |X[k]|²

Cutting a frame abruptly creates boundary discontinuities and spreads spectral energy into neighboring bins. A smooth analysis window reduces this leakage at the cost of a wider main lobe. Zero-padding makes the sampled spectrum denser; it does not create new physical frequency resolution beyond the observed frame duration.

Stage at 8 kHzFrame / hopWindow and transform
Noise suppression32 ms / 8 ms256 samples, Hann, 256-point FFT
Post-capture endpoints20 ms / 10 ms160-sample RMS/energy and sign-change analysis
MFCC25 ms / 10 ms200 samples, Hamming, zero-pad to 256-point FFT
Low-band heuristicabout 64 ms / half-frame512 samples, Hann, 512-point FFT for ordinary speech lengths

These grids serve different purposes. The streaming recording-stop detector works at the native input rate and uses its own 20 ms frames. It decides when to stop collecting audio. The post-capture endpoint detector later selects the speech region for feature extraction. Neither operation should be confused with the 10 ms MFCC feature hop.

Source: spectral_subtract_noise.m · hybrid_endpoint_detect.m · extract_mfcc_dsp.m · check_liveness_lowfreq.m

Chapter 07

Ambient spectral subtraction and reconstruction

The student stays quiet while the microphone records the room. The suppression stage averages the power spectra of frames from the initial ambient interval and uses that estimate in every frame of the utterance. This assumes the noise remains sufficiently similar after the profile; changing competing speech is much harder.

Pnoise[k] = mean over ambient frames of |X[k, frame]|²
Pclean[k,t] = max(|X[k,t]|² − 2 Pnoise[k], 0.02 Pnoise[k])
Ypositive[k,t] = sqrt(Pclean[k,t]) exp(j angle(X[k,t]))

The implementation subtracts power, despite older comments sometimes calling it magnitude subtraction. Oversubtraction by 2 trades remaining noise for possible speech distortion. The 0.02 floor retains a small noise-related residual rather than setting all negative estimates to zero. This can reduce isolated spectral peaks called musical noise, but it does not guarantee artifact-free sound.

The noise frames use a Hann window and a quarter-window hop. At 8 kHz the nominal half-second interval includes 63 frame starts under the implemented counting rule. A window beginning near the interval's end extends beyond it, which is one reason to respect the speaking-cue cushion rather than starting speech exactly at 0.5 s.

Returning from the spectrum to a waveform

For a real waveform, negative-frequency bins are the conjugate mirror of positive-frequency bins. The code reconstructs this Hermitian symmetry, applies the inverse FFT, multiplies by the synthesis window, and adds overlapping frames. It divides each output sample by the accumulated squared window weight. This compensates overlap gain where the window has nonzero support; zero-weight endpoints are guarded numerically.

The original phase is retained. The MFCC extractor later uses magnitude-derived power, but phase still matters to waveform reconstruction; keeping it is an approximation, not proof that phase is irrelevant to every signal-processing task. A stationary Wiener option shares the same profile and reconstruction and applies a signal-to-total-power gain instead of direct oversubtraction.

An SNR increase on synthetic additive noise does not establish improved speaker verification or cafeteria-babble cancellation. Read feature distances and recognition outcomes as well as waveform error.

Source: spectral_subtract_noise.m · experiment_synthetic_stress.m

Source: synthetic_noise_results.csv

Chapter 08

Speech endpoints: energy, zero crossings and run rules

After noise processing, endpoint detection finds a contiguous region from the first to the last accepted speech frame, with context padding. It does not identify words. Keeping every loud burst would confuse an impact with speech; rejecting all quiet sound can remove consonants. The implemented test combines level and sign-change behavior, then applies temporal rules.

E[t] = mean(frame[t]²)
Z[t] = number of sign changes / (frame length − 1)
EnergyGate = max(4 NoiseEnergy,
                 NoiseEnergy + 0.02(max(E) − NoiseEnergy), 10 eps)
Active = (E > EnergyGate) AND (Zlow ≤ Z ≤ Zhigh)

The default 20 ms frame and 10 ms hop become 160 and 80 samples at 8 kHz. Sign changes use the Boolean test x ≥ 0. The ambient energy and crossing estimates normally come from the median of the pre-roll frames. If that interval is too short or looks like speech rather than quiet background, the archive-friendly estimator uses the tenth percentile of all frame energies and the median crossing rate.

At 8 kHz, the active lower crossing bound is 0.008. The upper bound is min(0.45, max(0.25, 2.5 × noiseZCR)). Rate experiments scale the fixed crossing bounds to preserve a comparable physical crossing-frequency band. Some stored parameter fields are historical; the equations here describe the bounds the function actually uses.

Next, internal inactive gaps of at most eight frame positions are bridged. Active runs shorter than three frames are removed. Finally, the extracted waveform extends 40 ms on each side where samples exist. With overlapping frames, three active frames span about 40 ms, not three separate 20 ms blocks. The first-to-last region preserves internal waveform samples rather than concatenating only the selected frames.

Low-frequency hum can have few zero crossings, and high-frequency interference can have many, but these are heuristics. Real speech can also be atypical. The archive has no independently annotated field speech boundaries, so field truncation accuracy remains unmeasured.

Source: hybrid_endpoint_detect.m · preprocess_template_audio.m

Source: synthetic_vad_results.csv

Chapter 09

The low-frequency ratio: a diagnostic, not proof of liveness

The proposal adds a band-energy check after speech detection. The implementation averages windowed periodograms across the detected speech region and compares low-band energy with a wider speech-band total. At 8 kHz, a typical 512-sample frame gives 15.625 Hz bin spacing and a half-frame hop.

r = sum P[k] for 20 ≤ f[k] ≤ 200 Hz
    ------------------------------------
    sum P[k] for 20 ≤ f[k] ≤ 3,800 Hz

The selected configuration accepts ratios from 0.00024 through 0.7, subject to sufficient duration and measurable energy. The lower limit can flag little low-frequency content; the upper limit can flag excessive rumble. Each frame has its mean removed before the transform, and the ratio begins above DC.

Pitch, the amount of voiced speech, the microphone, the room, noise and playback hardware can all change this ratio. A genuine voice need not have a fundamental below 200 Hz. A recording played through a loudspeaker can retain low-frequency energy. Also, 50/60 Hz electrical hum is inside the low band; excluding frequencies below 20 Hz does not remove mains hum.

No labeled live-versus-phone-replay set was supplied. Therefore, the implemented band test cannot be assigned a measured replay-detection accuracy from this corpus. It is a signal-quality/security heuristic that requires dedicated live and replay evaluation before stronger claims are made.

Source: check_liveness_lowfreq.m · preprocess_audio.m

Source: liveness_results.csv

Chapter 10

MFCC: turning changing spectra into speaker features

MFCCs are classical acoustic features that compactly describe the short-time spectral envelope. The selected front-end uses 25 ms Hamming-windowed frames and a 10 ms hop. At 8 kHz this is 200 samples per frame, 80 samples per step, and a 256-point FFT after zero-padding.

Mel filterbank and logarithm

Twenty-six triangular filters span the configured 300–3700 Hz band. Their centers are equally spaced in mel coordinates, concentrating resolution at lower frequencies. Each filter sums nearby FFT powers. The natural logarithm compresses dynamic range and turns a multiplicative spectral scale into an additive change.

mel(f) = 1127 ln(1 + f/700)
L[m,t] = ln(max(Σ B[m,k] |X[k,t]|², eps))

The bank uses 28 boundary/center points for 26 overlapping triangles. The upper frequency is clipped to Nyquist when necessary. MFCC therefore does not preserve every FFT bin or the original phase; it retains a compact summary that must be tested for speaker discrimination.

Cepstra, liftering and dynamics

The discrete cosine transform decorrelates the log-mel channels into cepstral coefficients. The first thirteen coefficients, including coefficient zero, are retained. A sinusoidal lifter with parameter 22 changes their relative weights. “Lifter” acts in the cepstral-index domain; it is not another waveform low-pass filter.

c[q,t] = DCT(log-mel energies), q = 0,…,12
Lifter[q] = 1 + 11 sin(πq/22)
Δc[t] = Σ(k=1,2) k(c[t+k] − c[t−k]) / 10
Feature[t] = [c[t]; Δc[t]; Δ(Δc)[t]]  → 39 dimensions

The derivative uses a ±2-frame regression window. At the ends, indices repeat the nearest available frame. Delta-delta is the same operation applied to delta. These terms describe changes through the utterance and give DTW local costs temporal information beyond a static spectrum.

The selected configuration keeps all three blocks at weight one, includes coefficient zero, and leaves cepstral mean/variance normalization, pitch, auxiliary spectral features and RASTA disabled. Those are experimental candidates, not additions that can be assumed beneficial. Optional mean subtraction can reduce stable channel offsets while also removing information that helps distinguish speakers in a small corpus.

Source: extract_mfcc_dsp.m · extract_features.m · mfcc_auxiliary_features.m · experiment_variants.m

Chapter 11

DTW: flexible alignment, constrained paths and stable computation

Two recordings of a phrase may have different durations and local speaking rates. Cross-correlation searches a global shift; DTW allows local stretches while preserving time order. Let sequence A have N frames and B have M, with a feature vector at each frame.

Local cost d(i,j) = ||A[:,i] − B[:,j]||₂
D(i,j) = d(i,j) + min(D(i−1,j), D(i,j−1), D(i−1,j−1))
D(0,0) = 0; unreachable borders = infinity
Reported distance = D(N,M) / (N + M)

The three predecessors advance A, B, or both. Paths cannot reverse time or arbitrarily jump frames. Dividing by N+M reduces the growth of raw accumulated cost with utterance length. It is the project's chosen normalization, not division by the actual path length. For example, raw cost 6000 with N=100 and M=120 yields 27.27.

The Sakoe–Chiba corridor

The selected fraction is 0.30. The actual half-width is the maximum of ceil(0.30 × max(N,M)), |N−M|+1, and one cell. Allowing at least the length difference keeps the endpoint reachable. The corridor limits extreme alignments, while an overly narrow band can reject genuine rate variation.

Unconstrained recurrence work is O(NM); feature-vector costs also depend on dimension. This implementation forms a complete local-cost matrix to use efficient vector operations, then updates only recurrence cells inside the corridor. The band therefore does not imply that all full-grid allocation or distance preparation disappears.

Why the optimized recurrence gives the same paths

Within a row, the left-neighbor dependence can be written as a prefix minimum. Let cⱼ be row costs, Sⱼ their cumulative sum, and Bⱼ the minimum of the up and diagonal entries. Then:

Dⱼ = Sⱼ + min over k ≤ j of (Bₖ − Sₖ₋₁)

cumsum and cummin perform this work in compiled array operations while preserving the allowed paths. However, subtracting large nearly equal cumulative values can erase tiny differences. The code falls back to the direct norm-based recurrence for nonordinary numeric types/ranges and very uneven local costs. Dedicated equivalence tests include identical, warped, extreme and cancellation-prone inputs.

A speed improvement is useful only if its numerical behavior preserves decisions. The saved corpus distances and the deployed scorer are checked for agreement. Neither this algebra nor a low distance establishes identity by itself: matching still needs the independently entered claim and calibrated separation from competitors.

Source: dtw_distance_dsp.m · test_dtw_equivalence.m · voice_match_scores.m

Chapter 12

From template distance to a verified account

Each active student has one eligible ID reference and one eligible Name reference, stored as 1.wav in the corresponding folder. The matcher extracts reference features with the same calibrated settings, compares the query with each student's eligible reference, and ranks students by score. The production scorer supports mean, median and minimum template aggregation; the deployed one-reference protocol uses the mean, which equals that reference's distance.

The winning student must be the independently entered claim. The system never replaces the claim with whichever student happens to rank first. Each phrase then has its own distance ceiling and runner-up margin floor:

PhraseDistance ceilingRunner-up margin floor
ID31.348170761.20070604
Name30.351024711.21235332
Winner = argmin over enrolled students of distance
Margin = runner-up distance / max(best distance, eps)
Accept phrase ⇔ winner = entered claim
                AND best distance ≤ phrase ceiling
                AND margin ≥ phrase floor
                AND meaningful finite competing evidence exists

A margin of 1 means a tie. A margin near one means the best and second-best identities are hard to separate. A large margin means the winner is farther from its nearest competitor, but it is still not a probability. The runner must be a different valid student with a finite, positive distance strictly larger than the best. A missing meaningful competitor cannot produce a confident grant.

The distance ceiling and the margin answer different questions. A best distance of 30 might be below a ceiling near 31, yet a runner at 31 gives only a 1.033 margin and should be rejected. The fact that the runner lies outside the distance ceiling never waives the margin requirement.

The ordered fallback decision

If ID passes, verification finishes immediately and Name is not captured. If ID fails, Name gets one attempt and must independently win the same claim and pass its own gates. A strong Name result can therefore verify after an ID failure; the two distances are never averaged. If Name also fails, the transaction ends with FAILED.

The Name fields are absent or NaN when skipped, not evidence of a perfect zero distance. A diagnostic script may score a stored Name independently even when the workflow would skip it; such columns must be labeled as diagnostics. Two different phrase winners can support different separately enumerated wrong claims under fallback, so the experiment reports claim-level and source-speaker-level error measures separately.

A threshold belongs to its feature definition, preprocessing, reference protocol and distance normalization. Switching frontends without the corresponding phrase calibration is refused. Values above are measured operating points for this experiment, not universal constants.

Chapter 13

Data roles, calibration and the meaning of an error rate

The applied import contains 190 recording copies and 31 active profiles: 29 complete sets from the upload and two existing profiles that fill the empty 148/149 uploads. The active three-take corpus has 186 recordings, two phrase types times three takes times 31 students. The additional four recordings for 2206135 remain provisional because that student has only one ID take.

Folder 134 is missing from the supplied range and 155 is empty. Speaker labels come from the supplied folders; exact display-name spelling is unverified. Roll 137 still needs authoritative full-name confirmation. These are evidence limits, not reasons to invent recordings or relabel speakers.

Original recording order and converted take numbers

In each complete uploaded sequence, recording positions 1–9 are the individual digits 1–9; position 10 is digit zero; positions 11–13 are the three full-name takes; positions 14–16 are the three full-ID takes; position 17 is the complete counting sequence. These are ordinal recording positions. Filenames can start at zero or use other offsets, so the printed filename number is not automatically the recording position.

The selected recordings for all 29 complete uploaded profiles—174 ID/Name files—were checked against this order and already matched it. The converted corpus calls the three selected files in each phrase 1.wav, 2.wav and 3.wav. The incomplete 135 sequence cannot be validated by assuming it contains all 17 positions and remains provisional. The preserved 148/149 references are outside this uploaded-order check.

RoleRecordingWhat may use it
EnrollmentTake 1 of each phraseReference library
DevelopmentTake 2 of each phraseFeature/operating-point selection
Final evaluationTake 3 of each phraseApply the already frozen selection

Twenty-one declared candidates examine rate, AGC, suppression, endpoints, MFCC derivatives, normalization, auxiliary features, RASTA, DTW bands and feature weights. Selection first minimizes accepted false claims, then genuine rejections. Candidate and phrase operating points are saved before final-split extraction; tied objectives preserve the declared candidate order. The selected configuration is current_dsp.

This is a retrospective recording-disjoint split. The recordings had been inspected previously; it is not untouched prospective validation. Distinct filenames do not establish distinct recording sessions, dates, devices or environments. All offline roles use the archive feature adapter, whose clipping/pre-roll policy is more lenient than a fresh live capture.

For N students: genuine claims = N
False claims = N(N−1)
FAR = accepted wrong claims / false claims
FRR = rejected genuine claims / genuine claims
Genuine acceptance = 1 − FRR
Closed-set WSAR = source speakers with any accepted wrong claim / N

For N=31, there are 31 genuine claims and 930 own-content wrong claims per mode. A wrong-claim trial presents student A's own ID/name while claiming account B. This does not reproduce A deliberately speaking B's phrases. It also does not measure unknown-speaker attacks or phone replay.

Closed-set wrong acceptance counts each actual speaker once, even if its ID and Name would independently accept two different wrong accounts. Raw Top-1 is a separate diagnostic: it reports usable ID ranking in ID-first fallback, and Name ranking in Name-only mode. A successful Name fallback does not retroactively change the ID Top-1 result.

Chapter 15

Ablations, speed and what “better” means

The full fallback processing sum has a saved mean of 445.63 ms, median 460.32 ms and standard deviation 109.17 ms, across 93 repeated measurements. It sums separately measured ID and Name processing. When ID verifies immediately, the live system skips Name.

These wall timings exclude microphone capture, disk input, GUI interactions, network work and meal/payment operations. They do not measure average live session latency. Repeating the same recording measures compute variation; it does not add independent speakers. The sample-count reduction from resampling and a local DTW optimization benchmark must not be presented as a measured senior-to-final speedup.

On development recordings, 8 kHz fallback accepted 31/31 genuine claims, the fixed-band 16 kHz candidate 27/31, and fixed-band 44.1 kHz 24/31, with no accepted wrong claims at their selected development operating points. Several candidates tie the winning objective. The result supports the chosen configuration for this development set; it does not establish a universal sample-rate law.

The original senior source and matched execution environment are unavailable. The proposal and preserved legacy scripts describe a baseline using pre-emphasis and energy-only endpoints, but a current-code energy-only ablation is not an execution of that senior project. The five implemented modifications are RMS/rate control, low-band heuristic, ambient suppression, STE+ZCR endpoints, and meal-aware logging. Their implementation can be demonstrated even where field performance remains unmeasured.

Supplemental experiment: cross-correlation versus DTW

Four synthetic scalar feature sequences compare each query with its intended reference and one different event pattern. Both methods receive the same sequences. Cross-correlation searches the full range of global shifts; this supplemental DTW uses an unconstrained band and the project’s N+M normalization.

Timing conditionMatcherReference distanceDifferent distanceBest candidate
Identical timingCross-correlation00.640731Reference
Identical timingDTW00.302632Reference
Global shiftCross-correlation00.640731Reference
Global shiftDTW00.302632Reference

Uniform slowingDTW00.289474Reference

Uneven timingDTW00.304878Reference

Both matchers rank the intended reference first for identical timing and a global shift. In these constructed slowing and uneven-timing cases, cross-correlation ranks the different pattern first while DTW preserves the reference ranking. Cross-correlation uses one minus normalized correlation; DTW uses accumulated feature distance. Compare rankings within each method, not the magnitudes across methods. Values within floating-point roundoff of zero are displayed as zero.

This is a controlled alignment illustration using four synthetic queries and 16 query–template scores. It is not human-speaker accuracy, an execution of the unavailable senior implementation, or part of the frozen 31-student calibration. It does not show that DTW always wins on real recordings.

Chapter 16

Payment, time windows, duplicate prevention and audit records

Voice verification establishes an account, then the existing dining rules decide service. If the monthly dining fee is already recorded as paid, no new coupon is needed for that month. Otherwise, the operator supplies the assigned six-digit code. A code must belong to the verified student and the relevant month; it is not a way around the voice check.

Meal windows use local datetime values and configured start/end minutes. Each interval is half-open:

Meal is open ⇔ start minute ≤ current minute < end minute
Duplicate key = normalized student ID + date + meal name

The exclusive ending prevents two adjacent windows from both including their shared boundary. The actual schedule is data, not a second set of numbers printed into the GUI. Always read the current footer or configured schedule when demonstrating the system.

MealStartHourStartMinuteEndHourEndMinute
Breakfast70930
Lunch1201630
Dinner1902130

The meal logger checks existing records for the same student, calendar date and meal before appending. A second attempt in the same window is refused; the next meal window may be allowed. Biometric success, service permission and a successful CSV write are separate events. A verified student can still be refused because payment is missing, the window is closed, or the meal was already served.

The attempt log records the claim, outcome, available distances and margins, and the reason/stage. A skipped Name must not be treated as a successful zero-distance Name. Offline diagnostic runs skip business writes and should be interpreted through their biometric Verified result; they do not establish that a meal was served.

CSV is readable and practical for a laboratory demonstration. The read-check-append sequence is not demonstrated as an atomic transaction across multiple counters. Concurrent deployment would need coordinated locking or a transactional store, along with operational access control and a clear policy for resolving disputed transactions.

Chapter 17

Operating the project and understanding its tests

Run and explain one transaction

  1. Open the existing project folder in MATLAB and run run_meal_system.
  2. Enter the intended seven-digit account. Press Record and Verify, remain quiet for the ambient interval, and speak the whole ID after the cue.
  3. Allow recording to stop after the detected pause. Speak Name once only if requested.
  4. Read the final identity result and the separate service/payment outcome. If both voice attempts fail, the result is FAILED; press Record and Verify only to begin a new transaction after the previous one has finished.
  5. Use Instant Stop to cancel. It must not leave a second transaction running or permit a meal write after cancellation.

Different tests answer different questions

EvidenceQuestion it answersWhat it does not establish
Synthetic DSP diagnosticDo known signals exercise expected resampling, gain, endpoint, feature and logging behavior?Population verification accuracy
Capture-state testsDo onset, pause, cap and native-rate sample timing follow the state rules?Real-room microphone endpoint accuracy
DTW equivalence testsDoes optimized distance preserve the reference recurrence within tested numeric tolerances?All possible floating-point inputs
Claim/GUI regressionsAre gates, fallback, cancellation and reentry handled as specified?Voice quality of an unrecorded speaker
Frozen recording experimentWhat happened to these known genuine and wrong claims?Prospective session, spoof or field-noise performance
Deployment auditDo actual loaded profiles/gates reproduce the saved scores and decisions?Operational success at multiple simultaneous counters

run_meal_system('check') runs the software/DSP diagnostic. The deployed enrollment and calibration audit has separate saved outputs. Never relabel a prerecorded file test as a live microphone demonstration. Use a dedicated demonstration copy for meal/payment writes if the evidence package must remain unchanged.

When changing the system, alter one justified component, test its behavior, calibrate using development evidence, freeze the selection, then evaluate. Do not tune thresholds to repair the one known final rejection and still call the same final set an independent test. If the profile set or feature definition changes, the previous thresholds need new evidence.

Chapter 18

Glossary and questions for a teacher discussion

TermMeaning in this project
Sample rateWaveform samples per second, not feature frames per second.
RMS / energyRMS is the square root of mean squared amplitude; the endpoint energy statistic is mean squared amplitude.
SNRA signal/reference-to-noise power ratio; field SNR needs appropriate ground truth.
DFT / FFTThe mathematical finite Fourier transform / an efficient algorithm to compute it.
Mel / cepstrumA frequency scale / transformed log-spectrum coefficients.
DeltaA short-time regression derivative across feature frames.
DTWA monotone time alignment minimizing accumulated local feature distance.
MarginRunner-up distance divided by best distance; separation, not probability.
FAR / FRRAccepted false claims divided by false claims / rejected genuine claims divided by genuine claims.
Enrollment / calibrationStored reference evidence / development-time selection of operating points.
Verified / servedIdentity gates passed / business checks and meal logging succeeded.
RetrospectiveData were already available/inspected; results are not untouched prospective validation.

Why not accept the nearest student automatically?

Every nonempty ranked list has a nearest entry, including a bad recording or an impostor. The entered claim, absolute ceiling and separation margin prevent “nearest” from becoming automatic authorization.

Why does correct Top-1 still sometimes fail?

The winning identity may be correct but too distant or too close to a competitor. Rejection is an intended outcome when the evidence is weak. Conversely, Name fallback may verify after an incorrect ID ranking, so fallback genuine acceptance can exceed raw ID Top-1.

Why not record each digit separately?

The intended interaction is one natural whole-ID phrase, followed by a whole name only if needed. DTW handles timing variation inside the phrase. Separate digit enrollment and digit classification would be a different design and would change both user effort and evaluation assumptions.

Why keep a maximum duration if speech end is detected?

Continuous noise, no speech or an undetected ending can prevent the silence rule from firing. The cap bounds recording time; it does not turn a failed capture into valid identity evidence.

What would make the evidence stronger?

New recording sessions and microphones, deliberate same-content false claims, unknown speakers, labeled live/replay trials, real dining-hall noise conditions, and independently annotated speech endings would test the remaining uncertainties. More trials should add new conditions and speakers rather than merely repeat the same files.

Textbook connections: discrete-time sampling and multirate filtering; short-time spectral analysis and overlap-add; cepstral feature extraction; dynamic programming for sequence alignment; and statistical decision thresholds. The source-linked formulas above describe this implementation, including its practical guards and normalization choices.
